what: The sections of this article, each with a line and a paragraph, for showing what the reader has already read. Built by admin/build/summaries.py from admin/content/articles/summaries/.

sections.label: The opening
sections.line: A small security firm's grand website is read by buyers who won't hire it and unreadable to those who need it.
sections.para: A one-to-five person firm selling a SOC, XDR, red teaming and audits reaches security experts, who buy from established providers, and loses small businesses, who cannot read it: 9% of UK micro businesses knew Cyber Essentials in 2025. Sell at the right altitude: name the people, place and price, and sell outcomes an owner understands. A vault shows bad, medium and good versions of one invented firm.

sections.label: In short
sections.line: The grand website, the tragic symmetry, the 9%, the right altitude, the people, three questions, and a vault.
sections.para: Every service has to pass: sold it, can deliver it, readable by the buyer who needs it.

sections.label: The grand website
sections.line: A small firm's website that sells everything, cheap to build with AI, and the bigger it sounds the smaller it is.
sections.para: A dark theme, big numbers, a gradient headline and placeholder logos; larger firms show their people, history and scale instead.

sections.label: The tragic symmetry
sections.line: Experts who understand the page buy elsewhere; small businesses who need the firm cannot read it.
sections.para: A security lead buys a SOC from an established provider; the owner of a small practice leaves intimidated. 9% of UK micro businesses knew Cyber Essentials and 39% outsourced security at all.

sections.label: The right altitude
sections.line: Same work, different altitude: sell outcomes a small business owner understands.
sections.para: Open after ransomware, nobody logging in as you, laptops looked after, client data handled, AI tools doing what you meant. Agents now let three people check many clients' basics every day.

sections.label: Three versions of the same firm
sections.line: One invented firm, three websites: bad, medium and good, with how three readers see each.
sections.para: Bad reaches only the expert who will not buy; medium lists services and hides people; good names three people, a town, five outcomes, a price and what they do not do.

sections.label: Name the people
sections.line: Name the people: who answers the phone, who visits, where you are, and what it costs.
sections.para: A small firm's strongest asset is being small, and hiding behind a corporate voice throws it away.

sections.label: Three questions for every service
sections.line: Three questions for every service: have we sold it, can we deliver it at this size, would the buyer understand?
sections.para: If any answer is no, it is a claim, not a product: take it off, or say who you would send the customer to.

sections.label: Ask the readers, before the market does
sections.line: Synthetic users read the page as the buyer would, before the market does.
sections.para: An invented owner says quickly what a grand website means to her: she has no idea what it is.

sections.label: What this does not claim
sections.line: The firm and readers are invented; the curves are illustrative; the 9% and 39% are measured.
sections.para: Some small firms sell one specialism well; regulated businesses need more than the fundamentals.

sections.label: Where this comes from
sections.line: Dinis's conversation, DSIT's Cyber Security Breaches Survey 2025, the NCSC's small organisations guide, and the vault.
